content: Sixty minutes after insecticide application, the external door of the aircraft is opened, and the area is ventilated before entry. The number of mosquitoes knocked down is counted, and the cages are then removed from the aircraft. Mosquitoes from each cage are transferred as quickly as possible into individually marked, clean holding cups containing a 10% sugar solution on cotton wool. These cups are maintained for 24 hours at a temperature of 27°C ± 2°C and relative humidity of 80% ± 10%. The average percentage of female mosquitoes knocked down after 60 minutes and the average mortality rate after 24 hours are calculated based on pooled data from multiple test replicates. Before testing, an equivalent number of control cages are placed in the same locations, held for 60 minutes, and then removed from the aircraft. These control mosquitoes are also transferred into clean holding cups and observed under the same conditions for 24 hours to monitor mortality. If mortality in the control group exceeds 20%, the test is invalidated. For passenger cabin studies, the evaluation of products designed for rapid action and limited residual activity on aircraft surfaces involves separate assessments of these two effects. Rapid action is evaluated using the cage bioassay method described above, while residual activity is assessed immediately after the cage bioassay by conducting additional surface contact bioassays. The product must be applied throughout the cabin by trained personnel following the manufacturer’s instructions. According to WHO disinsection guidelines, all toilet doors, garment storage lockers, and overhead luggage compartments should be open, the air-conditioning system turned off, and the outer door closed during application. Residual activity is evaluated one hour after application using WHO cones secured to sentinel sites in the aircraft. These cones are placed on specified surfaces in three areas of the main passenger cabin: the middle row of seats, the fifth row from the front, and the fifth row from the rear. For single-aisle aircraft, WHO cones are secured with strong, non-marking tape at 11 locations on both the left and right sides of the cabin, including the floor of the overhead luggage compartment, the horizontal surface of the window seat, and the carpet beside the aisle seat. For dual-aisle aircraft, additional cones are placed on the middle seat and central seating area carpet. One hour after treatment, 10 non-blood-fed, 2–5-day-old female mosquitoes are introduced into plastic WHO cones secured at each location. The mosquitoes are exposed to treated surfaces for 30 minutes, then transferred into clean holding cups with a 10% sugar solution and held for 24 hours under controlled conditions. A minimum of three replicates from separately reared mosquito batches are tested per location, and results are pooled for analysis. Control bioassays are conducted in the same manner and locations before testing the residual effect of insecticides. If control group mortality exceeds 20%, the test results are rejected. Residual treatments should only be conducted by professional pest control operators. Aircraft out of service are preferred for testing to avoid interference from cleaning or maintenance activities, which could affect bioassay outcomes. Residual activity is monitored weekly until 24-hour mortality falls below 80%. Control tests are performed at weekly intervals by fixing small pieces of non-permeable plastic sheeting onto the cabin walls and placing six WHO cones on the sheeting. Ten non-blood-fed, 2–5-day-old female mosquitoes are introduced per cone for 30 minutes, then transferred into clean holding cups with a 10% sugar solution and held for 24 hours. Mortality is recorded after this period, and tests are rejected if control group mortality exceeds 20%. For cargo holds, fewer WHO cones are required due to the uniformity of interior surfaces. A minimum of six cones are placed in different locations, with one cone fixed on each wall and two on the ceiling. Residual activity is monitored weekly until 24-hour mortality falls below 80%. Control tests are performed similarly to those in passenger cabins. The WHO currently recommends three methods for aircraft disinsection: blocks away, preflight and top-of-descent spraying, and residual treatment. Blocks away spraying is conducted by crew members after cabin doors are closed and before takeoff, using an aerosol insecticide for rapid action. The air-conditioning system should be turned off during spraying, and overhead luggage rack doors should remain open until spraying is complete. Top-of-descent spraying is performed as the aircraft begins its descent to the arrival airport, using an aerosol containing 2% d-phenothrin. Residual spraying involves applying insecticide to the internal surfaces of the passenger cabin and cargo hold, excluding food preparation areas, using a compression sprayer with a constant flow valve and flat fan nozzle. The emulsion is applied at 10 mL/m² to avoid runoff, with intervals not exceeding two months. Residual sprays are intended for long-term activity and should be applied by professional pest control operators. In electrically sensitive areas, aerosol application may be necessary instead of compression spraying. All pesticide formulations, including spray cans, must comply with national regulations, international standards, and WHO specifications. Spray operations should adhere to international regulations, WHO-recommended procedures, and quarantine requirements in the destination country.
